description: CS seniors from Zagazig University, Egypt, specializing in .NET & React. We’re building a real-time health monitoring platform for astronauts on long-duration missions, tracking physical and mental well-being and flagging early warning signs before they become emergencies. Every alert explains why a crew member is at risk, and the system keeps working offline under Mars-level communication delays. Stack: ASP.NET Core, SignalR, React (PWA), PostgreSQL.
summary:
AstroCare is a web-based prototype designed to help astronauts monitor their health during space missions, where access to medical support from Earth can be limited or delayed.

Our application brings health readings, trends, and alerts into one accessible interface. Users can record measurements, review changes over time, and explore an interactive 3D body visualization to make health information easier to understand. AstroCare also includes reminders and a mental well-being support section, recognizing that astronaut health involves both physical and psychological needs.

By organizing health information and highlighting readings that may need attention, AstroCare aims to support crew awareness and more informed communication with ground teams. It is a monitoring and information tool, not a replacement for medical professionals. Our goal is to make everyday health tracking clearer and more accessible, helping astronauts focus on their mission.
details:
AstroCare – Onboard Health Monitoring for Deep-Space Crews
Team Lunaries · NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026 · Challenge: Health Monitoring Software

THE PROBLEM
On a Mars mission, a message to Earth and back can take up to 24 minutes, and there is no doctor on board. Astronauts are not physicians, yet they must notice early warning signs themselves. Generic “normal ranges” also miss what matters most: a heart rate of 74 bpm is normal on Earth, but not for an astronaut whose personal baseline is 63.

OUR SOLUTION
AstroCare is an offline, on-device health companion for astronauts. It compares every reading with the astronaut’s own baseline, not only with population ranges, catches small changes early, shows which part of the body is affected on an interactive 3D model, and tells the crew exactly what to do now, without waiting for Earth. Every alert explains the rule that fired, the threshold, the recommended action and the scientific source behind it.

HOW IT WORKS

  • Mission console: mission day and time (MET), live Earth communication delay, crew of four, open alerts and a one-tap Emergency button.
  • Mission environments: ISS, Moon, Mars transit and Mars surface. Switching changes the Earth delay, daily radiation dose and bone-loss rate across the whole app.
  • Interactive 3D body (Three.js): real anatomy where each organ system (heart, mind and sleep, bones, metabolism, radiation) is colored by its health status. Tap a part to focus on it and see its readings and alerts.
  • Three ways to record vitals: manual entry with validation, a simulated smart watch (built on the same interface a real wearable will use), and photo capture with on-device OCR.
  • Guided measurement: for each vital, why it matters in space, how to measure it step by step, how microgravity affects it and which signs are dangerous.
  • Daily check-in: sleep, mood, stress, exercise, water, meals and 18 symptoms. Five red-flag symptoms open Emergency mode immediately.
  • Personal baseline and trends: each chart shows the general normal range and the astronaut’s own 7-day baseline band, so drift is visible early.
  • Combined insights: the app links signals, e.g. “heart rate is rising while sleep is falling” or “headache while cabin CO2 is above the NASA limit: likely CO2-related”.
  • Emergency mode: step-by-step protocols, including a microgravity CPR metronome (Evetts-Russomano method). “Act now. Do not wait for Earth.”
  • Mind support: when mood is low or stress is high, it suggests NASA’s behavioral-health countermeasures.
  • Reminders and Earth report: daily routines, and a crew status summary for ground medical teams.

DEMO STORY (Omar Farid, flight engineer, 10 days)
Day 1 builds his baseline. Day 6: heart rate 74 bpm, still “normal”, but above his 63.4 baseline three days in a row, so AstroCare raises an early warning. Day 9: poor sleep, a headache and cabin CO2 at 3.2 mmHg (NASA limit 3) are linked into combined insights. Day 10: low water intake. A built-in day-by-day player replays the story.

NASA DATA AND SCIENCE
Health domains follow NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight (RIDGE): Radiation, Isolation and confinement, Distance from Earth, Gravity, and Hostile/closed environments. Rules and thresholds come from NASA Human Research Program risk pages (bone, cardiovascular, fitness, sleep, SANS, immune), NASA OCHMO technical briefs (radiation, CO2, life support), NASA space radiation data, and Canadian Space Agency radiation and space-medicine resources.
In numbers: 28 data-driven rules · 34 cited sources (17 NASA, 4 CSA, 6 peer-reviewed, 6 medical guidelines) · 6 vitals · 18 symptoms · 2 emergency protocols · 6 reminders · 4 mission environments.

TECHNOLOGY
React + Vite, Three.js / React Three Fiber for the 3D body (BodyParts3D anatomy, CC BY-SA), Zustand for state, and Zod-validated JSON for all data, rules and sources. No backend: it runs fully offline and saves readings in the browser (LocalStorage). The analysis logic is separate from the UI, so real sensors and wearables can plug in later. GitHub for version control, deployed on Vercel.

IMPACT
In space: earlier detection, clearer self-care and better-informed conversations with ground teams on long missions to the Moon and Mars.
On Earth: the same baseline-first approach fits people far from a doctor: Antarctic stations, offshore rigs, remote villages and elderly people living alone.

DESIGN APPROACH
A calm, dark mission console where color is used only for meaning: green for normal, amber for watch, red for action. The astronaut gets a quick view; the crew medical officer can drill into trends, rules and sources.

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS
AstroCare supports awareness and does not diagnose or replace medical care. Some thresholds are estimates and are labeled as such. Next: clinical validation of the rules, usability testing with analog-mission crews, real wearable integration, and evaluation under realistic mission conditions.
